pedagogy.summary: At 7–9 the eye is taught as a light-processing sequence plus one live response. The sequence: light enters through the pupil (the black opening), the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back of the eye, the retina detects the light and the optic nerve carries signals to the brain, which INTERPRETS them into what we 'see'. The live response is the pupil reflex — the pupil widens in dim light to let more in and narrows in bright light to let less in — which children can watch in a mirror or a partner's eyes. Two ideas do the heavy lifting: seeing is a chain that ends in the BRAIN (the eye detects, the brain interprets — you see 'with' your brain), and the pupil is a hole whose size changes, not a coloured part. Keep it to these named parts and the light→brain chain; avoid lens-physics detail. This builds directly on light being what eyes detect (from the five-senses topic) and feeds the nervous-system topic via the optic nerve.
bestPractices: Trace the light's journey in order (pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → brain), each part named by the ONE job it does, so seeing is a sequence, not scattered labels.
Demonstrate the pupil reflex live: watch pupils shrink when a light is shone and widen in the dark (in a mirror/partner), so the response is observed, not told.
Stress that the brain INTERPRETS the signal — the eye detects light, the brain makes the picture — to correct 'the eye sees'.
Clarify pupil vs iris: the pupil is the changing HOLE that lets light in; the iris is the coloured ring that changes its size.
Keep to the named parts and functions; leave lens focal-length and inversion detail for later (an inverted-image aside can intrigue but isn't required).
keyRepresentations: Eye cross-section with the light path arrowed pupil→lens→retina and the optic nerve to the brain
A light ray traced through the eye to a spot on the retina
Pupil-reflex demo: pupil large in dim light, small in bright light
The eye–brain link: retina signals travelling up the optic nerve to be interpreted
commonMisconceptions: 'The eye sees / makes the picture' — missing that the eye detects light and the BRAIN interprets it.
'Light comes OUT of the eyes to see things' — the ancient 'extramission' idea; light goes INTO the eye.
'The pupil is a black dot/part' — rather than an opening that lets light in and changes size.
'The pupil changes colour' — confusing the pupil (the hole) with the iris (the coloured ring).
'The lens is like glasses that magnify' — rather than focusing light onto the retina.
'You see the whole scene instantly and perfectly' — missing that the retina detects and the brain assembles the image (sets up illusions later).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach the eye as an ordered light-processing chain that ends in the brain, plus one live observable response: the pupil reflex. Children trace light pupil→lens→retina→optic nerve→brain (each part named by its one job), observe the pupil changing size with brightness, and learn that the eye DETECTS light while the brain INTERPRETS it into what we 'see'. Core conceptual targets: seeing is a sequence ending in the brain (not the eye alone), the pupil is a hole whose size changes (not a coloured part), and light travels INTO the eye (not out of it). Keep to named parts; leave lens focal-length/inversion physics for later.

activities.title: Drive the light's journey through the eye
feedback: If a learner says 'the eye sees the picture', add the final step: the retina only detects light and sends signals up the optic nerve; the BRAIN makes the picture — you see 'with' your brain.
If a learner treats the parts as a list, ask them to re-order the journey so each step depends on the one before.
At the extremes, prompt: in very bright light the pupil shrinks to let less in; in dim light it widens to gather more.
If a learner describes the pupil as a coloured dot, clarify: the pupil is the opening (the hole); the coloured ring around it is the iris, which changes the hole's size.
If a learner thinks the lens magnifies like a magnifying glass or like glasses, clarify its one job is to focus light into a sharp image on the retina, not to enlarge the image.

To push the brain's role further, ask: once the light and lens have done their job, what turns the pattern on the retina into actually SEEING a dog rather than a blur? Draw out that the brain interprets the signal into the recognised image.
activities.rationale: A model the child can drive makes both the reflex and the sequence observable and causal rather than merely told. A labelled diagram alone cannot animate the pupil responding or the light focusing, though it remains a good naming reference. Changing brightness and watching the pupil respond makes the 'pupil is a changing hole' idea observable. The brightness slider and brain-icon are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tools.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should build on earlier work about light and how we see things; sight is understood as light entering the eye and the eye/brain interpreting it, with named parts (pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve).
Light enters the eye through the pupil, is focused by the lens onto the retina, which sends signals via the optic nerve to the brain; the pupil constricts in bright light and dilates in dim light.
learnerActions: Starting from a light source, trace the path in order and name each part by its one job: pupil (lets light in), lens (focuses light), retina (detects light), optic nerve (carries signals), brain (interprets the picture).
Using a model or diagram where brightness can be changed (e.g. a slider), make the light dim and bright and watch the pupil widen and narrow in response.

Follow light rays streaming through the pupil, the lens bending them to a sharp focus on the retina, and a signal firing up the optic nerve to a brain icon that 'lights up' with the interpreted image.
Tap or point to each part to pause and state its single job; push the light to 'too dim' and 'too bright' extremes and say why the pupil adjusts.
Say in your own words what the eye does versus what the brain does.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing is a causal chain, not scattered labels: light enters, is focused, is detected by the retina, and only becomes the picture you 'see' when the brain interprets the signal. The pupil is a hole that changes size to control how much light enters.

activities.title: Watch the pupil reflex live (predict–observe–explain)
feedback: Keep the light moderate and aimed near, not straight into, a partner's eyes; the hands-cupped method is a safe light-free alternative.

Many children predict pupils widen in bright light; careful observation usually shows they shrink in bright light and are wide right after the dark (the change can be quick, small, or hard to see in dark-coloured eyes, so look closely and repeat if needed). Use the surprise to anchor the correct direction.
If a learner reverses the response, re-state: bright → smaller (protect the eye and limit light), dim → bigger (gather more light), and have them watch again.
Probe with a transfer case: walking from bright sunshine into a dim room — what happens to your pupils and why?
activities.rationale: A live predict–observe–explain cycle lets the response be seen rather than asserted, and the pre-observation reason reveals whether the child understands the pupil as a light-control opening. The common reversed prediction is productive because the direct observation contradicts it. Moderate light and the hands-cupped alternative keep the demonstration safe.
sourceClaims: Light enters the eye through the pupil, is focused by the lens onto the retina, which sends signals via the optic nerve to the brain; the pupil constricts in bright light and dilates in dim light.
learnerActions: In pairs in a normally lit room, predict whether your partner's pupils will get BIGGER or smaller when a moderate light (an ordinary torch or room light turned toward them — never shone directly into the eyes at close range) is used, and say WHY before looking.

As a gentler alternative that needs no extra light, have your partner cup their hands over their eyes for about 20 seconds, then uncover, and predict what their pupils will look like the instant they uncover.
Observe what actually happens, then compare it with your prediction.
Explain the result: what is the pupil doing, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: The pupil shrinks in bright light (to let less in) and widens in dim light or right after darkness (to gather more). The pupil is a light-control opening whose size is automatically adjusted.

activities.title: Which way does light travel? The dark-room argument
feedback: If a learner says eyes send out rays or beams to see (extramission), reverse the arrow: light travels from lit or reflecting objects into the eye. Use the dark room as proof — if eyes sent out rays, you'd see even with no light present.
If a learner thinks you could see in the dark by opening your eyes wide enough, establish that no light in means nothing for the retina to detect; adapting to dim light still needs SOME light.

A complete answer: light comes from the object (bounced off it, or given off if it is a light source like a lamp), enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina, the retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image.
For the glowing-cat case, note the eye is reflecting light back, not producing light to see with — the direction is still into the eye.
activities.rationale: The dark-room case discriminates the deep extramission misconception: a child who thinks eyes emit rays predicts you should still see if you 'try hard', while a child with light going INTO the eye explains the darkness correctly. Forcing a committed direction prevents a fudged answer.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should build on earlier work about light and how we see things; sight is understood as light entering the eye and the eye/brain interpreting it, with named parts (pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve).
learnerActions: Consider: in a completely dark room with no light at all, you can't see a thing even with your eyes wide open. Explain why not.
Commit to a direction: does light travel OUT of your eyes onto things, or FROM things INTO your eyes? Say which, and give your reason.
Explain the full account of how you end up seeing an object, from the object to the picture in your mind.
Discuss a tricky case: a cat's eyes seem to 'glow' in the dark — does that mean the cat's eyes make their own light to see with?
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing needs light to travel from objects INTO the eye; the eye is a receiver, not an emitter. With no light entering, the retina has nothing to detect — which is why a dark room is unseeable.

activities.title: Pupil, not iris: name the opening
feedback: If a learner says the pupil is a black dot or 'part', clarify it is an opening you look through into the eye.
If a learner says the pupil changes colour, separate the two: the pupil (hole) changes size; the iris (coloured ring) is what's coloured and what does the adjusting.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing the pupil-as-hole from the iris-as-coloured-ring directly targets a common confusion and supports the 'pupil is a changing opening' idea built in the other activities. The cited claim supports that the pupil is the opening light enters through; the iris naming is standard anatomy added to resolve the misconception.
sourceClaims: Light enters the eye through the pupil, is focused by the lens onto the retina, which sends signals via the optic nerve to the brain; the pupil constricts in bright light and dilates in dim light.
learnerActions: Look at your own eyes in a mirror, or at a partner's eyes, and point to the pupil (the black opening) and the iris (the coloured ring).
State which part is the HOLE that lets light in and which is the coloured ring that changes the hole's size.
Explain what changes when the pupil 'gets bigger' — is it a colour change or a size change of the opening?
activities.intendedInsight: The pupil is an opening (a hole) that lets light in and changes size; the iris is the coloured ring that adjusts it. The pupil does not change colour.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, match, and predict
feedback: If the sequence is muddled, return to the journey and ask what each step needs from the one before.
If the pupil prediction is reversed, re-anchor with the live observation: bright → smaller, dim → bigger.
If a part is matched to the wrong job, restate the single job of each named part.
activities.rationale: A clean consolidation check (sequence, part→job match, pupil prediction) confirms the core without lens-physics detail. Recognition and ordering tasks consolidate and can assess the core but do not by themselves elicit the full spoken explanation — pair them with the explain-and-justify activities above.
sourceClaims: Light enters the eye through the pupil, is focused by the lens onto the retina, which sends signals via the optic nerve to the brain; the pupil constricts in bright light and dilates in dim light.
learnerActions: Put the light path in the correct order: pupil → lens → retina → optic nerve → brain.
Match each part to its one job (pupil—lets light in; lens—focuses light; retina—detects light; optic nerve—carries signals; brain—interprets the image).
Given a light level (bright or dim), predict whether the pupil will be smaller or bigger and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can reliably name the parts, order the sequence, and predict the pupil's response by light level.

constraints: Keep to the named parts (pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, brain) and the light→brain chain; avoid lens focal-length and image-inversion physics. An inverted-image aside can intrigue but is not required.
Builds on light being what eyes detect (five-senses topic) and feeds the nervous-system topic via the optic nerve.

A labelled cross-section with tap-to-reveal parts teaches naming and the light path but cannot animate the pupil responding or the light focusing; use it as a companion reference, not a replacement for observing the reflex.
Ordering/matching/prediction tasks consolidate and can assess the core but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a full spoken explanation; include explain-and-justify tasks too.

A 3D eyeball could show the spherical shape and where the retina sits; it is optional for orientation. The causal ideas (light path, pupil reflex, eye→brain) can be served well in 2D — do not treat 3D as necessary, nor as adding nothing; it offers a different spatial view.
The brightness slider, brain-icon and live recolouring are optional illustrations that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory.

Safety: when demonstrating with real light, use ordinary room or torch light turned toward — not shone directly into, at close range — a partner's eyes, and keep brightness moderate. State this to learners in the activity; offer the hands-cupped-then-uncover method as a light-free alternative.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited sources are marked verified:false in the row; treat the pupil-direction and sequence claims as standard reference content pending verification.

The legacy entry asserted a static diagram 'cannot' make the reflex/sequence causal and that 3D 'adds nothing'; the universal/necessity framing is not established by the two sources and has been softened to scoped observable affordances and limits.
The original probe 'what turns the retinal pattern into seeing a dog rather than a blur?' is retained in activity 1 feedback to keep the brain-interpretation step explicit.

The pedagogy's lens-magnify misconception was absent from the candidate activities and has been restored to activity 1 feedback (lens focuses, does not enlarge); neither cited claim explicitly rebuts magnification, though both state the lens focuses light onto the retina.
Added explicit eye-safety wording to the live light demonstration; shining a bright light directly into children's eyes at close range should be avoided, and a light-free alternative is provided.

Self-audit: the pupil response direction (bright→constrict/smaller, dim→dilate/bigger) is stated consistently across summary, insights, feedback and notes; the reversed-direction version appears only as a misconception to correct, never as a valid learner answer. The extramission 'see in the dark' ideas are presented only as errors to refute, and light direction is consistently INTO the eye.

assess.poeTask: In pairs in a normally lit room, ask the child to predict whether their partner's pupils will get BIGGER or smaller when a bright light is shone toward them (or when the partner cups their hands over their eyes for 20 seconds, then uncovers), and to say WHY before looking. Many predict pupils widen in bright light; observation shows they shrink in bright light and are wide right after the dark. The pre-observation reason reveals whether they understand the pupil as a light-control opening.
probeDeeper: A cat's eyes seem to 'glow' in the dark. Does that mean the cat's eyes are making their own light to see with?
When you walk from bright sunshine into a dim room, what happens to your pupils, and why?
After the light and lens have done their job, what turns the pattern on the retina into you actually SEEING a dog rather than a blur?
assess.correctAnswer: You can't see in the dark because seeing needs light to travel FROM objects INTO your eyes — your eyes don't send anything out. Light bounces off the object, enters through the pupil, the lens focuses it onto the retina at the back, and the retina sends signals along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image. With no light entering, the retina has nothing to detect.

errorPatterns.pattern: Your eyes send out rays or beams to see things (extramission).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reverse the arrow: light travels from lit or reflecting objects INTO the eye; the eye is a receiver, not an emitter. Use the dark room as proof.
errorPatterns.distractor: Your eyes send out invisible rays that touch the object so you can see it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the eye emits something toward the object to see it.

errorPatterns.pattern: You could see in the dark if you just opened your eyes wide enough — seeing doesn't need light entering.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that no light in means nothing for the retina to detect; adapting to dim light still needs SOME light.
errorPatterns.distractor: You could see if you opened your eyes wide enough — seeing doesn't need light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Thinks the eye can adjust to see with no light present.

errorPatterns.pattern: The pupil gets bigger in bright light and smaller in dim light (reversed).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Correct the direction: pupil shrinks in bright light to protect the eye, widens in dim light to gather more; observe it directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses the pupil's response to brightness.

errorPatterns.pattern: The eye itself 'sees' the picture — no role for the brain interpreting the signal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the final step: the retina sends signals via the optic nerve and the brain interprets them into what you 'see'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stops the account at the retina or eye, with no brain interpretation.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the eyes send out rays, or that you could see in the dark; the direction of light is wrong.
responseLevels.full: States light travels from object into the eye (no emission), traces pupil→lens→retina→optic nerve→brain interpreting, and explains the pupil widens in dim light — justifying it with the dark room and a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Knows light enters the eye and can name parts, but muddles the sequence, reverses the pupil response, or leaves out the brain interpreting the signal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a completely dark room with no light at all, you can't see a thing, even with your eyes wide open. Why not? For seeing to happen, which way does the light have to travel — out of your eyes onto things, or from things into your eyes? Explain how you end up seeing an object.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The dark-room case exposes the deep extramission error — a child who thinks eyes send out rays predicts you should still see if you 'try hard'. Only a child who has light going INTO the eye explains the darkness correctly. The tier-two 'which way does light travel' forces the direction to be committed, not fudged.
